nodes.name: Copy principle
nodes.statement: Hume holds that every simple idea is copied from an earlier impression, a lively perception from the senses or from inner feeling.

nodes.name: Impression test
nodes.statement: Hume argues that the way to check a philosophical term is to ask from which impression its idea was copied. A term with no such impression has no clear meaning.

nodes.name: Hume's fork
nodes.statement: Hume divides all objects of human reasoning into two kinds: relations of ideas and matters of fact.

nodes.name: Relations of ideas
nodes.statement: For Hume, relations of ideas, such as truths of geometry and arithmetic, are known by thought alone. Denying one of them implies a contradiction.

nodes.name: Matters of fact
nodes.statement: For Hume, the contrary of every matter of fact is still possible, because it implies no contradiction.

nodes.name: Causation grounds factual inference
nodes.statement: Hume argues that all reasoning about matters of fact beyond present senses and memory rests on the relation of cause and effect.

nodes.name: Adam and water
nodes.statement: Hume claims that Adam, newly created with perfect reason, could not have inferred from the look of water that it would suffocate him.

nodes.name: No a priori causes
nodes.statement: Hume argues that no cause can be known by reason alone to produce its effect, because the effect is a distinct event from the cause.

nodes.name: Causes known by experience
nodes.statement: Hume concludes that knowledge of cause and effect comes only from experience.

nodes.name: Constant conjunction
nodes.statement: Hume holds that experience shows only that events of one kind have regularly been followed by events of another kind.

nodes.name: Uniformity assumption
nodes.statement: Hume argues that every inference from past experience to the future assumes that the future will resemble the past.

nodes.name: Tomorrow's sunrise
nodes.statement: Hume observes that the proposition that the sun will not rise tomorrow is just as intelligible as the proposition that it will rise, and implies no more contradiction.

nodes.name: Uniformity is not provable
nodes.statement: Hume argues that no demonstration can prove that nature is uniform, because a change in the course of nature implies no contradiction.

nodes.name: Circular support
nodes.statement: Hume argues that arguments from experience cannot support the uniformity assumption, because every such argument already relies on it.

nodes.name: Problem of induction
nodes.statement: Hume concludes that inferences from observed to unobserved matters of fact are not founded on reason.

nodes.name: Billiard balls
nodes.statement: Hume observes that when one billiard ball strikes another, an observer sees the first ball move, the contact and the second ball move. The observer sees no power that links them.

nodes.name: The will shows no power
nodes.statement: Hume argues that even when a person moves a limb, the person feels the act of will and sees the motion but never perceives the power that joins them.

nodes.name: No impression of power
nodes.statement: Hume argues that no single observed case of cause and effect gives an impression of necessary connection or power.

nodes.name: Repetition changes the mind
nodes.statement: Hume notes that many repeated cases contain nothing in the objects that a single case lacks. Repetition changes only the mind that observes them.

nodes.name: Custom or habit
nodes.statement: Hume argues that after repeated conjunctions, custom carries the mind to expect the usual effect as soon as it sees the cause.

nodes.name: Felt determination
nodes.statement: Hume argues that the mind feels its own customary move from cause to expected effect. This inner feeling is the impression from which the idea of necessary connection is copied.

nodes.name: Necessity is in the mind
nodes.statement: Hume concludes that necessity is something that exists in the mind, not in the objects.

nodes.name: Projection onto objects
nodes.statement: Hume claims that the mind has a great propensity to spread itself on external objects. So it ascribes to them a necessity that it only feels.

nodes.name: First definition of cause
nodes.statement: Hume defines a cause as an object followed by another, where all objects similar to the first are followed by objects similar to the second.

nodes.name: Second definition of cause
nodes.statement: Hume also defines a cause as an object followed by another, whose appearance always carries the thought to that other.

nodes.name: Belief as feeling
nodes.statement: Hume holds that belief differs from merely imagining an idea only by a more lively, firm and steady feeling attached to it.

nodes.name: Causal belief as instinct
nodes.statement: Hume argues that causal expectation is a natural instinct, which no reasoning can either produce or prevent.

nodes.name: Mitigated scepticism
nodes.statement: Hume recommends a mitigated scepticism. It keeps causal reasoning in daily life and science but limits inquiry to subjects that fit the narrow reach of human understanding.

nodes.name: Meaning of “power”
nodes.statement: Hume argues that words like “power” and “necessity” get their only meaning from the felt determination of the mind, not from any quality observed in objects.
